identity.name: SPARK
identity.tagline: Know where you stand. Know where to invest.
identity.description: A 27-item assessment that measures a leader's readiness to capture AI productivity gains across three interconnected layers: individual tool adoption, awareness of AI capability shifts in their domain, and organisational governance maturity. Leaders receive a composite AI readiness score, dimension-level verdicts, and a personalised archetype that describes their current relationship with AI at work.
identity.ideal_use_case: Leadership teams preparing for AI transformation; senior leaders assessing their own AI fluency gap; organisations benchmarking AI readiness before capability investment; pre-hire or pre-promotion assessment for technology-forward roles.

instrument_spec.delivery_format: Online self-assessment with instant HTML report
instrument_spec.scoring_method: Dimension-level normalised scores (0–20 each) + composite percentile (0–100)

dimensions.name: Individual AI Adoption Readiness
dimensions.description: Measures how deeply AI tools are integrated into the leader's own professional workflow — from occasional experimentation to systematic adoption, including their judgment to evaluate AI output quality and restructure established workflows.
dimensions.what_high_means: The leader uses AI tools deliberately and systematically, can evaluate output quality independently, and actively restructures workflows around AI capability.
dimensions.what_low_means: AI use remains experimental or absent; the leader has not developed reliable judgment about AI output quality and resists workflow change.

dimensions.name: Capability Exposure Assessment
dimensions.description: Measures the leader's awareness of what AI can and cannot do in their specific professional domain — including which of their own capabilities are at risk, which are becoming more valuable, and how their organisation compares to key partners.
dimensions.what_high_means: The leader has a current, detailed understanding of AI capabilities in their domain, has assessed personal and organisational capability exposure, and can identify AI asymmetry with counterpart organisations.
dimensions.what_low_means: The leader is uncertain about AI's current capabilities in their domain, has not assessed which skills are at risk, and is unaware of AI adoption gaps between their organisation and key partners.

dimensions.name: Organisational Preparedness
dimensions.description: Measures the maturity of the leader's organisation on AI governance — including tool usage policies, output review processes, data infrastructure, workforce capability development, and strategic clarity about which capabilities to build.
dimensions.what_high_means: The organisation has formal AI governance, clear tool policies, output review processes, quality data infrastructure, and invests in workforce AI capability development — not just tool procurement.
dimensions.what_low_means: The organisation lacks formal AI governance, data infrastructure is inadequate for systematic AI deployment, and AI investment focuses on tool access rather than workforce capability building.

axes.description: Combined signal from D1 (Individual AI Adoption Readiness) and D2 (Capability Exposure Assessment) — the leader's personal fluency and awareness
Signal from D3 (Organisational Preparedness) — the maturity of the organisation's AI governance, policy, and capability infrastructure

archetype_framework.note: The 3rd dimension (Capability Exposure Assessment) feeds into the Individual AI Readiness axis but is reported separately for diagnostic precision.

archetypes.name: AI Champion
archetypes.matrix_quadrant: High Individual Fluency × High Governance Maturity
archetypes.core_pattern: Drives AI adoption as a strategic priority across the organisation
strengths: Personally fluent with AI tools and domain capabilities
Operates within a mature governance structure
Can advocate for AI investment with credibility
growth_areas: Risk of over-advancing AI ahead of organisational absorption capacity
May create friction with less-ready stakeholders
Needs to balance speed with institutional readiness
archetypes.development_focus: Channel advocacy into structured change management; build coalition across readiness levels; calibrate pacing to organisational capacity.

archetypes.name: Skeptical Expert
archetypes.matrix_quadrant: High Individual Fluency × Low Governance Maturity
archetypes.core_pattern: Understands AI deeply; questions whether the organisation can manage it well
strengths: Strong personal AI judgment and domain fluency
Realistic about what AI can and cannot do
Identifies genuine governance and quality risks
growth_areas: Skepticism can slow or block legitimate AI adoption
May undervalue incremental progress toward governance maturity
Risk of disengagement when organisational policy lags behind capability
archetypes.development_focus: Channel critical thinking into building governance structures rather than blocking adoption; become a design partner for AI policy and quality assurance.

archetypes.name: Policy-First Adopter
archetypes.matrix_quadrant: Low Individual Fluency × High Governance Maturity
archetypes.core_pattern: Operates in a well-governed AI environment but has not built personal fluency
strengths: Works within clear AI policies and review processes
Organisation provides structural support for AI adoption
Lower risk of unregulated AI use
growth_areas: Governs or oversees AI without deep personal understanding of what it can do
May over-rely on process rather than expert judgment
Risk of falling behind peers who combine fluency with structure
archetypes.development_focus: Build hands-on AI fluency in their specific domain; learn to evaluate AI output quality directly; develop personal workflow integration before relying on policy alone.

archetypes.name: Unprepared Leader
archetypes.matrix_quadrant: Low Individual Fluency × Low Governance Maturity
archetypes.core_pattern: Neither personally fluent nor supported by organisational structure — significant AI capability gap
strengths: Awareness of the gap is the first step; growth potential is high
No bad habits to unlearn from ungoverned experimentation
growth_areas: At structural disadvantage relative to AI-ready peers
Risk of making poor decisions about AI investment and policy
Team and organisational performance will increasingly reflect the gap
archetypes.development_focus: Start with foundational AI literacy and personal tool adoption; simultaneously push for basic governance policies; address both individual and organisational levels in parallel.

composite_scoring.method: Three-dimension average of normalised scores, converted to 0–100 composite

bands.interpretation: Strong individual AI adoption, comprehensive capability awareness, and mature organisational governance. The leader and their organisation are positioned to capture AI productivity gains systematically.
Moderate AI readiness with meaningful gaps in at least one domain. Targeted investment needed to close specific capability or governance gaps.
Foundational AI capability is developing but not yet systemic. Risk of falling behind peers who are investing more deliberately in AI adoption.
Significant gaps across individual adoption, capability awareness, and organisational governance. Urgent investment required to avoid structural disadvantage.

dimension_verdicts.meaning: Mature capability with demonstrated organisational impact
Emerging capability with targeted development opportunities
Significant capability gap requiring immediate attention

sections: Strengths and growth areas per dimension
report_output.report_format: Interactive HTML report with visual dimension profile
